claim: The type 1 pilus rod structure was solved at 4.2 Å resolution using cryo-electron microscopy.
source: We solved the 4.2 Å resolution structure of the type 1 pilus rod using cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: The resolution is stated in the abstract and supported by FSC plots in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing resolution at FSC = 0.143.

claim: The type 1 pilus rod is a 70 Å diameter structure.
source: Overall, the type 1 pilus is a 70 Å diameter rod where each adjacent subunit rotates around the helical axis by 115° and translates along the axis by 7.7 Å (Figure 2A).
evidence: Direct measurement from the cryo-EM structure as stated in the Results section.

claim: Each adjacent FimA subunit rotates around the helical axis by 115° and translates along the axis by 7.7 Å.
source: Overall, the type 1 pilus is a 70 Å diameter rod where each adjacent subunit rotates around the helical axis by 115° and translates along the axis by 7.7 Å (Figure 2A).
evidence: Helical symmetry parameters determined from the cryo-EM reconstruction.

claim: Each FimA subunit interacts with six adjacent subunits (N-1, N-2, N-3, N+1, N+2, N+3).
source: If we label each subunit along the 1-start helix by N, a subunit N0 interacts with six adjacent subunits (N-1,N-2,N-3,N+1,N+2,N+3) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Structural analysis of subunit-subunit interactions in the cryo-EM model.

claim: Donor strand complementation in the type 1 pilus involves mostly hydrophobic interactions.
source: The donor strand complementation involves mostly hydrophobic interactions.
evidence: Observation from the cryo-EM structure showing hydrophobic residues at the interface.

claim: Val5, Val10 and Phe12 in the N-terminal β-strand of one FimA subunit are inserted into the next subunit's hydrophobic groove.
source: Most prominently, the hydrophobic amino acids Val5, Val10 and Phe12 in the N-terminal β-strand (Nte) of one subunit are inserted into the next subunit's hydrophobic groove created by a missing β-strand (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Structural details observed in the cryo-EM model showing specific residue interactions.

claim: Half of the FimA residues in the mature protein are invariant (79/161 residues).
source: Global alignment revealed a consensus sequence of 161 residues where half of the FimA residues in the mature protein are invariant (79/161 residues) and that 83.9% are highly conserved (139/161 residues with >95% sequence identity) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Analysis of 1,828 FimA protein sequences from the Ensembl Bacteria database.

claim: 83.9% of FimA residues are highly conserved (139/161 residues with >95% sequence identity).
source: Global alignment revealed a consensus sequence of 161 residues where half of the FimA residues in the mature protein are invariant (79/161 residues) and that 83.9% are highly conserved (139/161 residues with >95% sequence identity) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Analysis of 1,828 FimA protein sequences from the Ensembl Bacteria database.

claim: FimA sequences are significantly more variable than FimC chaperone and FimH adhesin sequences.
source: We found the FimA sequences to be significantly more variable than other parts of the type 1 pilus machinery. For example, the mature forms of the FimC chaperone and FimH adhesin (n = 1,760 and n = 1,943, respectively; Supplementary file 4) obtained from the same database contain 97.6% and 97.5% highly conserved residues, respectively, as compared to 83.9% in FimA.
evidence: Comparative sequence analysis of type 1 pilus components from the Ensembl Bacteria database.

claim: Non-conserved residues within FimA sequences are all located on the exterior surface of the pilus rod.
source: Interestingly, the non-conserved residues within the FimA sequences are all located on the exterior surface of the solved cryo-EM model (Figure 3B), which is likely indicative of immune pressures selecting for antigenic diversification (Wildschutte et al., 2004).
evidence: Mapping of sequence conservation onto the cryo-EM structure combined with citation to previous work on antigenic diversification.

claim: Almost every residue involved in subunit-subunit interactions in the rod is either highly conserved or invariant.
source: In contrast, almost every residue involved in subunit-subunit interactions in the rod is either highly conserved or invariant (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Mapping of sequence conservation data onto the structural model showing conservation at interaction interfaces.

claim: Every residue lining the lumen of the type 1 pilus is 100% conserved.
source: This includes every residue lining the lumen (Figure 3C).
evidence: Sequence conservation analysis mapped onto the structure, with Figure 3C showing all lumen-facing residues in blue (100% conserved).

claim: 66 codons in fimA were under purifying selection.
source: Here, we found that 66 codons were under purifying selection, five codons were under adaptive selection, and an additional 27 codons were too conserved to be included in analysis (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: dN/dS ratio analysis of 191 unique fimA sequences using fixed-effects likelihood measurement.

claim: Five codons in fimA were under adaptive selection.
source: Here, we found that 66 codons were under purifying selection, five codons were under adaptive selection, and an additional 27 codons were too conserved to be included in analysis (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: dN/dS ratio analysis of 191 unique fimA sequences using fixed-effects likelihood measurement.

claim: All positively selected sites in FimA (N64, A109, T117, S120 and F138) encode residues located on the exterior surface of the FimA rod away from subunit-subunit interfaces.
source: All of the positively selected sites, N64, A109, T117, S120 and F138, encode residues located on the exterior surface of the FimA rod and away from any subunit-subunit interface (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Mapping of positively selected sites onto the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The fimA gene was carried by 96.3% (26/27) of UPEC strains analyzed.
source: The fimA gene was carried by the majority of E. coli strains analyzed (57/67); including nearly every UPEC strain (96.3% or 26/27 strains).
evidence: BLAST-based search of 67 curated E. coli genomes.

claim: Three branches in the fimA phylogeny showed statistically significant evidence of episodic diversifying selection.
source: Here, we identified three branches with statistically significant evidence of episodic diversifying selection, including two branches carrying most of the clinical UPEC strains (branches labeled A and B) as well as enterohemorrhagic and enterotoxigenic E. coli strains in the branch labeled C (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Random effects likelihood ratio test for each branch of the fimA phylogenetic tree.

claim: Several FimA mutations (A25R, V32R, V65R, V85R, and P145R) abolished the production of adhesive pili.
source: However, several mutations (A25R, V32R, V65R, V85R, and P145R) abolished the production of adhesive pili (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: Hemagglutination assays of FimA mutants expressed in UTI89-LON∆fimA.

claim: Expression of FimA mutants V5R, E45R, E121R and A142R resulted in a bacterial clumping phenotype when grown in static culture.
source: Expression of some mutant fimA genes, particularly V5R, E45R, E121R and A142R, resulted in a bacterial clumping phenotype when grown in static culture.
evidence: Observation of bacterial cultures expressing mutant FimA proteins.

claim: The unwinding force of wild-type type 1 pili was 30.3 ± 0.2 pN.
source: The unwinding force of WT pili was 30.3 ± 0.2 pN (mean ±standard error (SE)) whereas all mutants showed a reduction in the force required for pilus unwinding (Figure 4B).
evidence: Optical tweezers measurements of single pilus unwinding force.

claim: All FimA mutants tested (A22R, A92R, D114R, D62R, K155R and P132R) showed a reduction in the force required for pilus unwinding compared to wild-type.
source: The unwinding force of WT pili was 30.3 ± 0.2 pN (mean ±standard error (SE)) whereas all mutants showed a reduction in the force required for pilus unwinding (Figure 4B).
evidence: Optical tweezers measurements comparing wild-type and mutant pili.

claim: The A22R FimA variant showed the largest reduction in unwinding force at 11.2 ± 0.2 pN.
source: In particular, the A22R variant showed the largest reduction in the unwinding force, 11.2 ± 0.2 pN.
evidence: Optical tweezers measurements of A22R mutant pili.

claim: Ala22 in the FimA rod model is tightly packed against Ala93 from another subunit and Val37 from a third subunit.
source: We can explain this by the fact that Ala22 in our rod model is tightly packed against Ala93 from another subunit and Val37 from a third subunit (Figure 4C).
evidence: Structural analysis of the cryo-EM model showing specific residue contacts.

claim: Strains producing FimA variants D62R, D114R, and A22R were outcompeted by up to six logs by the wild-type strain in chronically infected mice.
source: In mice that developed chronic cystitis (defined as the development of persistent high titer (>104 cfu/ml) bacteriuria and high titer (>104 cfu/ml) bladder bacterial burdens at sacrifice >4 weeks post-infection), strains producing FimAUTI89 variants with the D62R, D114R, and A22R substitutions were outcompeted by up to six logs by the reintegrated WT strain (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: Competitive infection experiments in C3H/HeN mice over 28 days.

claim: The FimA P132R variant had no effect on the ability of the strain to compete with the wild-type strain in chronically infected mice.
source: The FimA P132R variant had no effect on the ability of the strain to compete with the WT strain in chronically infected mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: Competitive infection experiments in C3H/HeN mice over 28 days.

claim: Wild-type UTI89 and P132R variant caused chronic cystitis at similar rates (45% and 30%, respectively).
source: In mice infected with a single UTI89 strain, the WT and P132R variant caused chronic cystitis at similar rates (45% and 30%, respectively) (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Single strain infection experiments in C3H/HeN mice over 28 days.

claim: The D114R and D62R mutant strains had reduced rates of chronic cystitis of 20% and 10%, respectively.
source: However, the D114R and D62R mutant strains had reduced rates of chronic cystitis of 20% and 10%, respectively.
evidence: Single strain infection experiments in C3H/HeN mice over 28 days.

claim: 100% of mice infected with the A22R variant resolved their infections over the 4 week experiment.
source: Interestingly, 100% of mice infected with the A22R variant resolved their infections over the 4 week experiment, with half of the mice (10/20) exhibiting sterile urines by 10 dpi compared to just 15% (3/20) of mice infected with the WT strain at the same time point (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Single strain infection experiments in C3H/HeN mice over 28 days with longitudinal urinalysis.

claim: Two FimA variants (A22R and D114R) significantly altered the ability of UTI89 to form IBCs at 6 hr post infection.
source: Accordingly, we found that two fimA variants (A22R and D114R) significantly altered the ability of UTI89 to form IBCs at 6 hr post infection (hpi) (Figure 5G), with 8/10 mice infected with the D114R variant forming <15 IBCs.
evidence: IBC enumeration in bladder wholemounts at 6 hpi.

claim: 70% of mice infected with the A22R variant formed no IBCs at 6 hpi and the other 30% formed three or less.
source: Even more strikingly, 70% of mice infected with the A22R variant formed no IBCs at 6 hpi and the other 30% formed three or less.
evidence: IBC enumeration in bladder wholemounts at 6 hpi.

claim: Wild-type and P132R strains formed between 50–100 IBCs on average by 6 hpi.
source: This is in stark contrast to WT and P132R strains, which formed between 50–100 IBCs on average by 6hpi.
evidence: IBC enumeration in bladder wholemounts at 6 hpi.

claim: The A22R mutant was severely attenuated in its ability to invade into bladder cells starting as early as 1 hr post infection.
source: Interestingly, the A22R mutant was severely attenuated in its ability to invade into bladder cells starting as early as 1 hr post infection (Figure 5H).
evidence: Bacterial invasion assays at 1, 3, and 6 hr post infection.

claim: Strains producing FimA variants D62R, D114R, and A22R showed lower levels of intestinal colonization (by up to 2 logs) compared to wild-type.
source: We found that strains producing FimAUTI89 variants D62R, D114R, and A22R showed lower levels of intestinal colonization (by up to 2 logs) in the feces, cecum, and colon of mice compared to those colonized by WT fimA (Figure 6).
evidence: Intestinal colonization experiments in streptomycin-treated C3H/HeN mice at 7 days post colonization.

claim: The 2-log decrease in intestinal colonization by FimA mutants mirrors the defect observed in UTI89Δfim or UTI89ΔfimH strains.
source: This 2-log decrease mirrors the defect observed in UTI89Δfim or UTI89ΔfimH strains, suggesting that these mutations prevent type 1 pilus-dependent gut colonization in UTI89 (Spaulding et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with previously published data on fim deletion mutants cited from Spaulding et al., 2017.

claim: Type 1 pili are critical virulence factors in uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC).
source: Arguably, the best-studied CUP pili are those encoded by uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC), which is the causative agent of the majority of urinary tract infections (UTIs).
evidence: Established knowledge about UPEC pathogenesis discussed in the Introduction.

claim: Type 1 pili facilitate bacterial colonization and subsequent invasion into epithelial cells lining the bladder lumen.
source: Upon entering the bladder, type 1 pili facilitate bacterial colonization and subsequent invasion into epithelial cells lining the bladder lumen (Mulvey et al., 1998; Martinez et al., 2000).
evidence: Cited from previous studies by Mulvey et al., 1998 and Martinez et al., 2000.

claim: Type 1 pili help mediate UPEC intestinal colonization.
source: Recent work has revealed that type 1 pili help mediate UPEC intestinal colonization, thus promoting the establishment and/or maintenance of the UPEC reservoir in the gut that can eventually seed UTI (Spaulding et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from recent work by Spaulding et al., 2017.

claim: UPEC that cannot invade the urothelium are quickly cleared from the bladder.
source: UPEC that cannot invade the urothelium, like those lacking type 1 pili or its associated adhesin, FimH, are quickly cleared from the bladder, emphasizing the importance of type 1 pili mediated host-pathogen interactions on the fitness of UPEC during cystitis (Wright et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited from Wright et al., 2005.

claim: After invading into a bladder cell, UPEC escape into the host cell cytoplasm and replicate to form biofilm-like intracellular bacterial communities (IBCs) comprised of ~10^4 cells.
source: After invading into a bladder cell, UPEC escape into the host cell cytoplasm and replicate to form biofilm-like intracellular bacterial communities (IBCs) (Anderson et al., 2003; Justice et al., 2004) comprised of ~104 cells (Wright et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from Anderson et al., 2003; Justice et al., 2004; and Wright et al., 2007.

claim: The type 1 pilus coils into a rigid right-handed helical structure that is capable of unwinding into a flexible linear fiber.
source: Once extruded to the extracellular surface, the type 1 pilus coils into a rigid right-handed helical structure that is capable of unwinding into a flexible linear fiber (Abraham et al., 1992; Jones et al., 1995; Saulino et al., 2000; Aprikian et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies: Abraham et al., 1992; Jones et al., 1995; Saulino et al., 2000; Aprikian et al., 2011.

claim: The type 1 pilus is proposed to act as a 'molecular spring' to maintain adherence in the face of fluid shear forces.
source: This ability to transition between a coiled, helical rod and a linear fiber has been proposed to allow the type 1 pilus to act as a 'molecular spring' to maintain adherence in the face of fluid shear forces (Zakrisson et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from Zakrisson et al., 2012.

claim: CUP pili are critical virulence factors in a wide range of pathogenic bacteria, including Escherichia, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Haemophilus, Salmonella and Yersiniae genera.
source: Notably, CUP pili are critical virulence factors in a wide range of pathogenic bacteria, including Escherichia, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Haemophilus, Salmonella and Yersiniae genera (Nuccio and Bäumler, 2007).
evidence: Cited from Nuccio and Bäumler, 2007.

claim: 38 distinct CUP pilus types have been identified in Escherichia and Shigella genomes and plasmids.
source: To date, 38 distinct CUP pilus types have been identified in Escherichia and Shigella genomes and plasmids, each of which is hypothesized to promote bacterial colonization of a distinct habitat (Nuccio and Bäumler, 2007; Wurpel et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Nuccio and Bäumler, 2007 and Wurpel et al., 2013.

claim: Single Escherichia coli genomes carry up to 16 distinct CUP operons.
source: Interestingly, single Escherichia coli genomes carry up to 16 distinct CUP operons, suggesting that the retention of an assortment of CUP pilus types by a single strain may be necessary to accommodate the complex lifecycle of E. coli (Wurpel et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Wurpel et al., 2013.

claim: UTIs affect 150 million people annually worldwide.
source: UTIs affect 150 million people annually worldwide and are associated with significant morbidity and economic impact (Foxman, 2014).
evidence: Cited from Foxman, 2014.

claim: ~25% of women suffer from recurrent UTI (rUTI).
source: UTI treatment failure is common, with ~25% of woman suffering from recurrent UTI (rUTI), and is due, in part, to the increasing prevalence of drug-resistant UPEC strains (Scholes et al., 2000; Zowawi et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Scholes et al., 2000 and Zowawi et al., 2015.

claim: The vast majority of sequenced E. coli strains, including nearly all sequenced UPEC clinical isolates, carry an intact copy of the type 1 pilus.
source: While the types of CUP pilus operons encoded in E. coli genomes varies between different clades and individual strains, the vast majority of sequenced E. coli strains, including nearly all sequenced UPEC clinical isolates, carry an intact copy of the type 1 pilus (Wurpel et al., 2013; Schreiber et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Wurpel et al., 2013 and Schreiber et al., 2017.

claim: The majority of UPEC strains isolated from women with UTI in the USA reside in the B2 clade.
source: While UPEC strains tend to be genetically heterogeneous the majority of UPEC strains isolated from women with UTI in the USA reside in the B2 clade (Schreiber et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Schreiber et al., 2017.

claim: The type 1 pilus rod is a homopolymer of ~1000 FimA subunits.
source: Following this pattern, the type 1 pilus usher (FimD) and chaperone (FimC) help type 1 pili assemble into a composite pilus structure consisting of a short tip fibrillum made up of the adhesin protein (FimH) and two minor subunits (FimG and FimF) that is joined to the pilus rod, a homopolymer of ~1000 FimA subunits.
evidence: Established knowledge about type 1 pilus structure discussed in the Introduction.

claim: The unwinding force measured for wild-type type 1 pili in this study is similar to what has been reported in the literature.
source: The unwinding force measured for WT type 1 pili in this study is similar to what has been reported in the literature (Andersson et al., 2007).
evidence: Comparison with previously published measurements cited from Andersson et al., 2007.

claim: Replacing alanine 22 with arginine is expected to disrupt the subunit interface due to steric clashes.
source: Thus, replacing a small alanine with a long arginine side chain is expected to disrupt this interface.
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis showing Ala22 is tightly packed against other residues.

claim: The pilus rod may act as a 'molecular spring' during mucus shedding in the gut.
source: In the gut, the pilus rod may play a similar role during mucus shedding.
evidence: Speculation based on the bladder findings extended to the gut environment.

claim: Type 1 pili may promote UPEC colonization of the upper crypts in the gut.
source: A recent study suggests that type 1 pili may promote UPEC colonization of the upper crypts (Spaulding et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Spaulding et al., 2017.

claim: The clumping phenotype caused by D62R and D114R mutations suggests these mutations may alter side-to-side interactions between different pilus rods.
source: However, the clumping phenotype suggests that these mutations may alter side-to-side interactions between different pilus rods promoting pilus-pilus interactions within and between bacteria, thus inhibiting the pilus mediated interactions needed in vivo for attachment, invasion and/or IBC formation.
evidence: Inference based on the observed clumping phenotype and structural location of the mutations.

claim: The type 1 pilus rod may mediate colonization phenotypes through damping of shear forces or through other mechanism(s) outside of scaffold support for FimH-binding.
source: Together, our data suggest that the type 1 pilus rod may mediate colonization phenotypes through damping of shear forces or through other mechanism(s) outside of scaffold support for FimH-binding.
evidence: Inference drawn from the combined in vitro and in vivo experimental results.

claim: A wild-type rod that could never uncoil would be susceptible to breakage by shear forces.
source: This would still suggest that the mechanical properties of these rods have been 'tuned' to optimize for particular environments, as a wt rod that could never uncoil would be susceptible to breakage by the shear forces, while a rod that uncoils too easily would be unnecessarily exposed to digestion by proteases.
evidence: Speculation about the evolutionary optimization of rod mechanical properties.

claim: A rod that uncoils too easily would be unnecessarily exposed to digestion by proteases.
source: This would still suggest that the mechanical properties of these rods have been 'tuned' to optimize for particular environments, as a wt rod that could never uncoil would be susceptible to breakage by the shear forces, while a rod that uncoils too easily would be unnecessarily exposed to digestion by proteases.
evidence: Speculation about the evolutionary optimization of rod mechanical properties.

claim: FimA displays patterns of episodic, divergent selection on surface exposed amino acids similar to what is seen in the flagellin protein in Salmonella.
source: FimA displays patterns of episodic, divergent selection on surface exposed amino acids in a pattern that is similar, though much less robust, to what is seen in the flagellin protein in Salmonella (Li et al., 1994).
evidence: Comparison with known patterns in Salmonella flagellin cited from Li et al., 1994.

claim: In Salmonella, the flagellin subunits are split into several domains where the domains responsible for subunit-subunit assembly are highly conserved while the more external domains show high rates of variability.
source: In Salmonella, the flagellin subunits are split into several domains where the domains responsible for subunit-subunit assembly are highly conserved while the more external domains of the protein show high rates of variability (Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005; Galkin et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005 and Galkin et al., 2008.

claim: Flagellin is bound by Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5) resulting in the induction of the innate immune response.
source: While it is known that flagellin are bound by Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5) resulting in the induction of the innate immune response (Smith and Ozinsky, 2002) and that this recognition is targeted towards conserved features of flagellin (Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005), it is currently unknown which, if any, host immune receptor are capable of recognizing the FimA rod or subunits or which structural features are targeted by the host immune system.
evidence: Cited from Smith and Ozinsky, 2002 and Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005.

claim: It is currently unknown which, if any, host immune receptor are capable of recognizing the FimA rod or subunits.
source: While it is known that flagellin are bound by Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5) resulting in the induction of the innate immune response (Smith and Ozinsky, 2002) and that this recognition is targeted towards conserved features of flagellin (Andersen-Nissen et al., 2005), it is currently unknown which, if any, host immune receptor are capable of recognizing the FimA rod or subunits or which structural features are targeted by the host immune system.
evidence: Statement of current knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The bacterial clumping phenotype is associated with mutation of three codons under purifying selection and an equal number of mutations in codons with little to no evidence of selective pressure.
source: For example, the bacterial clumping phenotype is associated with mutation of three codons under purifying selection, but an equal number of the mutations that resulted in clumping are in codons with little to no evidence of selective pressure.
evidence: Analysis of the relationship between phenotypes and selection pressure on codons.

claim: All mutations that failed to complement a fimA gene deletion were made in codons that are under very strong purifying selection or are too conserved for analysis.
source: In contrast, all mutations that failed to complement a fimA gene deletion were made in codons that are under very strong purifying selection or are too conserved for analysis.
evidence: Analysis of the relationship between phenotypes and selection pressure on codons.

claim: The mis-assembly of the pilus is much more harmful and/or toxic to E. coli than bacterial clumping.
source: Together, the difference in selection pressure suggests that the mis-assembly of the pilus is much more harmful and/or toxic to E. coli than bacterial clumping.
evidence: Inference drawn from the differences in selection pressure associated with different phenotypes.

claim: Many codons under purifying selection are involved in keeping the force needed to unwind the type 1 rod within a narrow range.
source: Instead, we found that many codons under purifying selection are involved in keeping the force needed to unwind the type 1 rod within a narrow range.
evidence: Integration of evolutionary analysis with optical tweezers measurements.

claim: A 'weak' or 'loose' FimA rod may be just as detrimental for E. coli as having no rod at all, at least in the eyes of evolution.
source: This leads to reasoning that a 'weak' or 'loose' FimA rod may be just as detrimental for E. coli as having no rod at all, at least in the eyes of evolution.
evidence: Inference drawn from the evolutionary analysis and functional studies.

claim: The mechanical properties of the type 1 pilus rod are essential for its functional role in mediating E. coli pathogenesis and persistence.
source: In summary, by combining structural studies, force spectroscopy, genetic analysis, and relevant mouse models of UTI and gut colonization, we conclude that the mechanical properties of the type 1 pilus rod are essential for its functional role in mediating E. coli pathogenesis and persistence and appear to have been carefully 'tuned' by evolution.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the integration of structural, biophysical, evolutionary, and in vivo experimental data.

claim: The mechanical properties of the type 1 pilus rod appear to have been carefully 'tuned' by evolution.
source: In summary, by combining structural studies, force spectroscopy, genetic analysis, and relevant mouse models of UTI and gut colonization, we conclude that the mechanical properties of the type 1 pilus rod are essential for its functional role in mediating E. coli pathogenesis and persistence and appear to have been carefully 'tuned' by evolution.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the integration of structural, biophysical, evolutionary, and in vivo experimental data.

claim: Type IV pili can elongate under force.
source: In addition, other bacterial pili, such as T4P, which have arisen independently of CUP pili but can play similar roles in pathogenesis, can also elongate under force (Biais et al., 2010) and thus it remains an interesting question as to how the physical properties of other pili have been selected for particular environments and how these properties impact bacterial pathogenesis.
evidence: Cited from Biais et al., 2010.

claim: There were no ambiguities in threading the known FimA sequence through the density map.
source: There were no ambiguities in threading the known FimA sequence through the density map (Supplementary file 1), even though the electron density observed on the outside of the rod is less well defined (Figure 1B).
evidence: Statement about the model building process and quality of the cryo-EM map.

claim: The first two residues and the last residue of FimA are not resolved in the density map.
source: As a result, the first two residues and the last residue of FimA, which are located close to each other on the outside of the rod, are not resolved in the density map.
evidence: Statement about limitations of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The 4.2 Å estimate of the resolution is consistent with the well-separated β-strands and the density present for certain bulky side chains in the central lumen.
source: The 4.2 Å estimate of the resolution is consistent with the well-separated β-strands and the density present for certain bulky side chains in the central lumen (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Assessment of map quality features that support the stated resolution.

claim: In the type 1 pilus structure, the N-terminal donor strand of one subunit completes the β-sheet of the adjacent subunit.
source: Further, in the structure we observe the N-terminal donor strand of one subunit completing the β-sheet of the adjacent subunit.
evidence: Direct observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: FimA residues 22–33 show structural differences between the cryo-EM rod structure and previously solved crystal structures of FimA.
source: Further, residues corresponding to FimABW2511322–33, which are part of the interior surface of the rod helix, show structural differences between our cryo-EM rod structure and the previously solved crystal structures of FimA (Crespo et al., 2012)(Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison of the cryo-EM structure with previously published crystal structures cited from Crespo et al., 2012.

claim: Within the cryo-EM rod FimA structure, residues 25–29 adopt a helical conformation.
source: Within the cryo-EM rod FimA structure, residues 25–29 adopt a helical conformation and residues 30–33 form a β-strand interaction with residues 10–13 from the Nte of the next FimA subunit.
evidence: Structural observation from the cryo-EM model.

claim: FimA residues 30–33 form a β-strand interaction with residues 10–13 from the Nte of the next FimA subunit.
source: Within the cryo-EM rod FimA structure, residues 25–29 adopt a helical conformation and residues 30–33 form a β-strand interaction with residues 10–13 from the Nte of the next FimA subunit.
evidence: Structural observation from the cryo-EM model.

claim: The ability of FimA residues 22–33 to adopt multiple conformations may be necessary for FimA to function as the major rod subunit.
source: These residues form the center strand within the hollow helical core, and thus the ability of this region to adopt multiple conformations may be necessary in order for FimA to function as the major rod subunit.
evidence: Inference based on structural observations and comparison with other FimA structures.

claim: The interface between subunits N0 and N+3 is extremely important in maintaining the FimA helical rod.
source: The interface between subunits N0 and N+3 is extremely important in maintaining the FimA helical rod.
evidence: Statement based on structural analysis of subunit interactions.

claim: Two atomic models (PDB ID: 2N2H and 2MX3) for the type 1 pilus have been generated using the same solid-state NMR data.
source: Previously, two atomic models (PDB ID: 2N2H and 2MX3) for the type 1 pilus have been generated using the same solid-state NMR data (Habenstein et al., 2015), with the helical symmetries for these models shown in Supplementary file 2.
evidence: Cited from Habenstein et al., 2015.

claim: The overall RMSD between Cα atoms of subunit N+3 in the cryo-EM model and 2N7H is 5.7 Å.
source: The overall RMSD between Cα atoms of subunit N+3 in our cryo-EM model and 2N7H is 5.7 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), while it is 11.0 Å with 2MX3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Structural comparison calculation between different models.

claim: The overall RMSD between Cα atoms of subunit N+3 in the cryo-EM model and 2MX3 is 11.0 Å.
source: The overall RMSD between Cα atoms of subunit N+3 in our cryo-EM model and 2N7H is 5.7 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), while it is 11.0 Å with 2MX3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Structural comparison calculation between different models.

claim: In the P pilus, residues 1–5 are fully ordered and make a 90° bend to form a 'staple' which involves contacts with two other subunits.
source: Comparison of our type 1 pilus model with the P pilus structure (Hospenthal et al., 2016) shows an interesting difference: in the P pilus, residues 1–5 are fully ordered and make a 90° bend to form a 'staple' which involves contacts with two other subunits (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Comparison with P pilus structure cited from Hospenthal et al., 2016.

claim: In the type 1 pilus, the first two residues are disordered and the remaining three residues in this region project straight out of the structure and make no contacts with other subunits.
source: In contrast, the first two residues are disordered in our type 1 pilus rod, and the remaining three residues in this region project straight out of the structure and make no contacts with other subunits (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Structural observation from the cryo-EM model compared with P pilus.

claim: Some FimA sequences contain an additional two amino acid residues at the N-terminus of the mature protein compared to BW25113.
source: Here, we found that many of the FimA sequences were comprised of 159 residues, including BW25113, while other FimA sequences, such as the one from UTI89, a prototypical UPEC isolate, contained an additional two amino acid residues at the N-terminus of the mature protein (Figure 3A).
evidence: Sequence alignment analysis of 1,828 FimA proteins.

claim: The degree of divergence between alleles of FimA is abnormally high compared to most E. coli genes.
source: In general, most E. coli genes evolve slowly (Lee et al., 2012), so the degree of divergence between alleles of FimA is abnormally high.
evidence: Comparison with general E. coli gene evolution cited from Lee et al., 2012.

claim: The selection forces acting on the FimA protein are different from the forces acting on the rest of the fim operon.
source: This suggests that the selection forces acting on the FimA protein are different from the forces acting on the rest of the fim operon.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of conservation levels between FimA and other fim operon components.

claim: The first few amino acids of the N-terminus of the mature FimA protein have some of the highest variability throughout the entire protein.
source: In particular, the first few amino acids of the N-terminus of the mature protein, disordered in our reconstruction, have some of the highest variability throughout the entire protein, suggesting that these amino acids do not play a functional role in the dynamics of unwinding in the type one pilus rod.
evidence: Sequence conservation analysis combined with structural observation.

claim: The N-terminal amino acids of mature FimA do not play a functional role in the dynamics of unwinding in the type one pilus rod.
source: In particular, the first few amino acids of the N-terminus of the mature protein, disordered in our reconstruction, have some of the highest variability throughout the entire protein, suggesting that these amino acids do not play a functional role in the dynamics of unwinding in the type one pilus rod.
evidence: Inference based on high sequence variability and disorder in the structure.

claim: The conservation of residues lining the lumen might be due to the transport of some product through the ~15 Å opening.
source: The conservation of residues lining the lumen might be due to the transport of some product through this opening that is ~15 Å across (the height of the triangular lumen that rotates as one travels along the pilus).
evidence: Speculation about the functional reason for conservation of lumen residues.

claim: Every residue in the lumen is either involved in making a subunit-subunit contact or packed tightly between residues that are making such contacts.
source: More likely, however, every residue in the lumen is either involved in making a subunit-subunit contact (including the DSE contacts with the Nte from an adjacent subunit) or packed tightly between residues that are making such contacts.
evidence: Structural analysis of residue positions and interactions in the lumen.

claim: FimAUTI89 differs from FimABW25113 in 16 residues, with all differences lying within highly variable residues located on the exterior of the pilus rod.
source: Thus, we do note that FimAUTI89 differs from our cryo-EM rod FimABW25113 sequence in 16 residues, with all of the differences lying within highly variable residues located on the exterior of the pilus rod, including two additional amino acids at the N-terminus.
evidence: Sequence comparison between FimAUTI89 and FimABW25113.

claim: 27 codons in fimA were too conserved to be included in evolutionary analysis.
source: Here, we found that 66 codons were under purifying selection, five codons were under adaptive selection, and an additional 27 codons were too conserved to be included in analysis (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: dN/dS ratio analysis of fimA sequences.

claim: 63 codons in fimA showed no evidence of statistically significant selection in either direction.
source: The remaining 63 codons showed no evidence of statistically significant selection in either direction.
evidence: dN/dS ratio analysis of fimA sequences.

claim: Evolutionary pressures are working to conserve the identity of residues that interact within the helical rod while diversifying amino acid residues exposed to the host.
source: This strongly suggests that evolutionary pressures are working to conserve the identity of residues that interact within the helical rod, while diversifying amino acid residues that are exposed to the host and susceptible to immune recognition.
evidence: Inference based on the pattern of purifying selection at interfaces and adaptive selection on surface residues.

claim: There is not a single variant of FimA found in all UPEC strains.
source: Importantly, the fimA sequences from UPEC strains were spread through the phylogenetic tree, indicating that there was not a single variant of FimA found in all UPEC strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis of fimA sequences from UPEC and other E. coli strains.

claim: fimA is much more diverse than other parts of the type 1 machinery, owing to high rates of nucleotide polymorphisms and genetic recombination.
source: Taken together, we find that fimA is much more diverse than other parts of the type 1 machinery, owing to high rates of nucleotide polymorphisms and genetic recombination, and that fimA has undergone repeated rounds of strong selective pressures that have conserved residues responsible for subunit-subunit interfaces while varying the external surface of the protein that is exposed to the host milieu.
evidence: Summary of evolutionary analyses including recombination detection and selection pressure measurements.

claim: fimA has undergone repeated rounds of strong selective pressures that have conserved residues responsible for subunit-subunit interfaces while varying the external surface of the protein.
source: Taken together, we find that fimA is much more diverse than other parts of the type 1 machinery, owing to high rates of nucleotide polymorphisms and genetic recombination, and that fimA has undergone repeated rounds of strong selective pressures that have conserved residues responsible for subunit-subunit interfaces while varying the external surface of the protein that is exposed to the host milieu.
evidence: Summary of evolutionary analyses showing patterns of selection.

claim: Mutations A25R, V32R, V65R, V85R, and P145R may disrupt critical interactions with FimC or FimD or may not be able to correctly fold.
source: This suggests that these mutations, which are located in areas of high conservation throughout the FimA monomer, may disrupt critical interactions with FimC or FimD or may not be able to correctly fold, thus preventing the assembly of the pilus.
evidence: Inference based on the loss of pilus assembly function and location of mutations in conserved regions.

claim: Residues A25, V85 and P145 were under strong purifying selection pressure.
source: Notably, each of these residues was either under strong purifying selection pressure (A25, V85 and P145) or was too conserved for evolutionary analysis (codons for V32 and V65 displayed no synonymous mutations and extremely limited non-synonymous mutation rates), which emphasizes their importance in assembly of the type 1 pilus rod (Figure 3A).
evidence: Evolutionary analysis showing selection pressure on specific codons.

claim: Codons for V32 and V65 displayed no synonymous mutations and extremely limited non-synonymous mutation rates.
source: Notably, each of these residues was either under strong purifying selection pressure (A25, V85 and P145) or was too conserved for evolutionary analysis (codons for V32 and V65 displayed no synonymous mutations and extremely limited non-synonymous mutation rates), which emphasizes their importance in assembly of the type 1 pilus rod (Figure 3A).
evidence: Evolutionary analysis showing extreme conservation of specific codons.

claim: D62R and D114R mutations instigated bacterial clumping to a lesser extent than V5R, E45R, E121R and A142R.
source: D62R and D114R also instigated bacterial clumping, but to a lesser extent.
evidence: Observation of bacterial cultures expressing mutant FimA proteins.

claim: Three substitutions (E45R, E121R and A142R) that caused clumping are found in residues with relatively high variability.
source: Three of these substitutions, E45R, E121R and A142R, are found in residues with relatively high variability in our analysis of FimA sequences, with just 33.9%, 62.3%, and 52.1% sequence identity, respectively.
evidence: Correlation of clumping phenotype with sequence conservation analysis.

claim: Residues V5 and D114 showed statistically significant evidence of strong purifying selection.
source: Further, we found that two of these residues (V5 and D114) showed statistically significant evidence of strong purifying selection (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Evolutionary analysis showing selection pressure on specific residues.

claim: Type 1 pili normally extend in three force phases: linearly increasing, constant force, linearly increasing.
source: Since type 1 pili are assembled from FimA subunits into a helical coil, they normally extend in three force phases: linearly increasing, constant force, linearly increasing – where the characteristic constant force originates from sequential unwinding of subunits (region between the dashed lines in Figure 4A).
evidence: Description of the characteristic force-extension behavior observed in optical tweezers experiments.

claim: The characteristic constant force in pilus extension originates from sequential unwinding of subunits.
source: Since type 1 pili are assembled from FimA subunits into a helical coil, they normally extend in three force phases: linearly increasing, constant force, linearly increasing – where the characteristic constant force originates from sequential unwinding of subunits (region between the dashed lines in Figure 4A).
evidence: Explanation of the physical basis for the constant force plateau based on established understanding of pilus mechanics.

claim: The unwinding force directly relates to the strength of layer-to-layer interactions between subunits N0 and N+3.
source: The unwinding force directly relates to the strength of layer-to-layer interactions (e.g., between subunits N0 and N+3), thus any changes in these interactions caused by mutations would shift the magnitude of the force plateau.
evidence: Inference based on the structural understanding of subunit interactions and mechanical properties.

claim: All FimA mutant strains demonstrated similar levels of GP-RBC agglutination compared to wild-type.
source: When compared to a strain with the reintegrated WT UTI89 fimA sequence, we found that all reintegrated FimA mutant strains demonstrated similar levels of GP-RBC agglutination, in vitro (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), despite some variability in the level of piliation between FimA mutant strain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Hemagglutination assays of chromosomal FimA mutants in UTI89.

claim: Some FimA mutants showed variability in the level of piliation.
source: When compared to a strain with the reintegrated WT UTI89 fimA sequence, we found that all reintegrated FimA mutant strains demonstrated similar levels of GP-RBC agglutination, in vitro (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), despite some variability in the level of piliation between FimA mutant strain (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Electron microscopy analysis of piliation levels in different strains.

claim: Mutants that show increased hemagglutination in the presence of exogenous mannose correlated with those that showed clumping in culture.
source: Interestingly, those mutants that show some increased hemagglutination in the presence of exogenous mannose compared to the WT strain correlated with those that showed some clumping in culture.
evidence: Correlation observed between two different in vitro phenotypes.

claim: The FimA mutations do not prevent the expression or function of type 1 pili in vitro.
source: Overall, these findings indicate that the FimA mutations, which reduced the unwinding force of the rod, do not prevent the expression or function of type 1 pili in vitro.
evidence: Summary of in vitro characterization showing pili are expressed and functional despite mutations.

claim: The defect in chronic infection caused by fimA variants is likely due to pathogenic deficiencies during acute UTI.
source: The defect in chronic infection caused by fimA variants is likely due to pathogenic deficiencies during acute UTI.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that chronic infection defects correlate with acute infection defects.

claim: The D62R variant was defective in chronic cystitis in both competitive and single bladder infections but no acute fitness defects were observed.
source: The D62R variant was defective in chronic cystitis in both the competitive and single bladder infections, but no acute fitness defects were observed.
evidence: Summary of infection experiments showing chronic but not acute defects.

claim: Mice infected with D62R formed a similar number of IBCs as the wild-type strain at 6 hpi.
source: Further, mice infected with D62R formed a similar number of IBCs as the WT strain at 6 hpi, suggesting that the defect occurs at a later time-point.
evidence: IBC enumeration showing no difference at 6 hpi.

claim: The defect in D62R occurs at a later time-point after 6 hpi.
source: Further, mice infected with D62R formed a similar number of IBCs as the WT strain at 6 hpi, suggesting that the defect occurs at a later time-point.
evidence: Inference based on normal IBC formation at 6 hpi but defects in chronic infection.

claim: In mice singly infected with fimA D62R, bacterial clearance is delayed, starting between 10–14 days.
source: Accordingly, in mice singly infected with fimA D62R bacterial clearance is delayed, starting between 10–14 days (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Longitudinal urinalysis data from single infection experiments.

claim: Type 1 pili promote the establishment and/or maintenance of the UPEC intestinal reservoir.
source: In addition to playing a pivotal role in the urinary tract, a recent study found that type 1 pili also promote the establishment and/or maintenance of the UPEC intestinal reservoir (Spaulding et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Spaulding et al., 2017.

claim: Deletion of the operon encoding the type 1 pilus or the FimH adhesin impedes intestinal colonization by UTI89.
source: Deletion of the operon encoding the type 1 pilus or the FimH adhesin impedes intestinal colonization by UTI89 (Spaulding et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from Spaulding et al., 2017.

claim: The fimA P132R variant showed lower colonization (by up to one log) in the feces and cecum than the wild-type strain, though not statistically significant.
source: While not statistically significant, fimAUTI89 P132R variant showed lower colonization (by up to one log) in the feces and cecum than the WT strain (Figure 6).
evidence: Intestinal colonization data showing a trend but no statistical significance.

claim: The sequence of the FimA major subunit is critical for pilus function in the bladder and gut.
source: Together, our data indicates that the sequence of the FimA major subunit is critical for pilus function in the bladder and gut and thus has a major impact on the outcome of UTI.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the combined bladder and gut colonization experiments.

claim: The sequence of the FimA major subunit has a major impact on the outcome of UTI.
source: Together, our data indicates that the sequence of the FimA major subunit is critical for pilus function in the bladder and gut and thus has a major impact on the outcome of UTI.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the combined experimental results.

claim: Cryo-EM allows for multiple conformations among particles or subunits to be separated and solved from the same micrographs.
source: The ability of cryo-EM to separate out multiple conformations among particles (Gui et al., 2017; Vonck and Mills, 2017) or even of subunits within the same particle (Roh et al., 2017) has been one of the greatest strengths of cryo-EM, allowing for multiple states to be solved from the same micrographs.
evidence: Cited from Gui et al., 2017; Vonck and Mills, 2017; and Roh et al., 2017.

claim: Biochemically heterogeneous preparations are now routinely sorted into homogeneous structural classes by cryo-EM.
source: Biochemically heterogeneous preparations, such as when virions are a mixture of empty particles and those containing DNA (Dong et al., 2017) are now routinely sorted out into homogeneous structural classes.
evidence: Cited from Dong et al., 2017 as an example of cryo-EM capabilities.

claim: Filament images that might otherwise have been discarded as background contaminant can be used to build an atomic model.
source: We have taken advantage of that strength here to show that filament images which might otherwise have been discarded as a background contaminant can actually be used to build an atomic model.
evidence: Description of the approach used in this study to solve the type 1 pilus structure.

claim: The type 1 pilus rod model provides new insights into structure-function relationships in type 1 pili.
source: Our type 1 pilus rod model provides new insights into structure-function relationships in type 1 pili.
evidence: Summary statement about the contribution of the structural work.

claim: The pilus formed by the FimA A22R mutant variant may not have the strength to absorb and withstand the shear forces experienced during urination.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that the pilus formed by the FimA A22R mutant variant may not have the strength to absorb and withstand the shear forces experienced during urination and thus allow the bacteria to be swept out of the bladder, preventing infection.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the reduced unwinding force and severe infection defects of the A22R mutant.

claim: Bacteria in the upper crypts would experience constant, low levels of shear force during mucus turnover.
source: These bacteria would likely experience constant, low levels of shear force during mucus turnover and thus need the pilus to withstand some force to enable the bacteria to maintain their intestinal niche.
evidence: Speculation about the physical forces experienced by bacteria in the gut environment.

claim: The phenotypes of the fimA mutants in gut colonization were not as severe as in the bladder.
source: However, in general, the phenotypes of the fimAUTI89 mutants in gut colonization were not as severe as in the bladder.
evidence: Comparison of colonization defects between bladder and gut experiments.

claim: The lower uncoiling force of the A22R mutant may expose parts of the rod that would be largely buried in the wild-type filament to host proteases.
source: A possibility that we cannot exclude at the moment is that the lower uncoiling force of the A22R mutant exposes parts of the rod that would be largely buried in the wt filament to host proteases.
evidence: Alternative hypothesis for the mechanism of A22R attenuation.

claim: It is exceedingly difficult to crystallize most helical polymers unless they have exactly two, three, four or six subunits per turn.
source: In particular, it is exceedingly difficult to crystallize most helical polymers, as unless such a polymer has exactly two, three, four or six subunits per turn, it cannot be packed in any crystal space group so that all subunits are in equivalent environments.
evidence: Explanation of crystallographic constraints for helical structures based on established crystallographic principles.

claim: Type 1 filaments present as a background in a preparation of T4P allow reaching near-atomic level of resolution.
source: We show here that type 1 filaments, present as a background in a preparation of T4P, allow us to reach a near-atomic level of resolution and build an atomic model for the FimA rod.
evidence: Description of the experimental approach and outcome.

claim: Three types of filaments could be separated by eye in the cryo-EM preparation: T4P, flagellar filaments, and type 1 pili.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, three types of filaments could be separated by eye: T4P, flagellar filaments, and a third class that were thicker and more rigid than T4P but thinner than the flagellar filaments.
evidence: Visual inspection of cryo-EM micrographs.

claim: The FimA amino acid sequence was identical to the FimA protein from BW25113 and MG1655.
source: Sequencing the fimA PCR product showed that the encoded amino acid sequence was identical to the FimA protein from BW25113 (GenBank AIN34588.1) and MG1655 (GenBank NP_418734.1).
evidence: DNA sequencing of the fimA gene from the preparation.

claim: There was no possibility of cross-contamination of the FimA and T4P filament images.
source: There was no possibility of cross-contamination of the FimA and T4P filament images, as each has a very different helical symmetry.
evidence: Explanation based on the distinct helical symmetries of the two filament types.

claim: Averaged power spectra from FimA filaments showed no trace of the Type IV pilus spectrum.
source: Averaged power spectra from FimA filaments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showed no trace of the Type IV pilus spectrum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Analysis of power spectra from the two filament types showing they are distinct.

claim: A total of 6803 cryo-EM images were collected.
source: A total of 6803 images, each of which was from a total exposure of 2 s dose-fractionated into seven chunks, were collected at a range of underfocus between 0.5 ~ 3 μm.
evidence: Description of data collection parameters.

claim: A total of 72,627 overlapping segments were used for the IHRSR reconstruction.
source: A total of 72,627 overlapping segments (384 px long), with a shift of 11 px between adjacent segments (~97% overlap), were used for the IHRSR (Egelman, 2000) reconstruction.
evidence: Description of image processing parameters.

claim: Approximately 55% of the segments were excluded due to having a twist outside of the range 114.4° to 115.6°.
source: Using a reference-based sorting with models having a fixed rise but a variable twist, approximately 55% of the segments were excluded, having a twist outside of the range 114.4° to 115.6°.
evidence: Description of the sorting and selection process during image processing.

claim: A subset of 32,726 segments were used for the final reconstruction cycles.
source: A sub-set of 32,726 segments were used for a few more cycles of IHRSR.
evidence: Description of the final dataset used for reconstruction.

claim: The Washington University Animal Studies Committee approved all procedures used for the mouse experiments.
source: The Washington University Animal Studies Committee approved all procedures used for the mouse experiments described in the present study.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval for animal experiments.
